 From Heavyweight to 42-Year-Old Middleweight Gatekeeper: The Evolution of Jared Cannonier’s UFC Run
 Originally posted on
 Athlon Sports 
  | 
 By Lois Ogunniyi
  | 
 Last updated Nov 19, 2026 11:39 AM ET
 Add us as a preferred source on Google
 When Jared Cannonier steps into the Octagon at ABHA Arena in Doha this Saturday, he will be making his 22nd UFC appearance—and facing a ranked contender at 42 years old.
 Few fighters have remained competitive at the highest level for this long. Even fewer have done it after dropping approximately 65 pounds across three different weight classes.
 Ahead of his UFC Qatar clash with Ikram Aliskerov, Cannonier’s career represents one of the most unusual transformations in modern MMA. But after four defeats in his last five fights, his latest challenge raises a bigger question: is the former title challenger approaching the end of his UFC career?
 Three Weight Classes, One Cannonier 
 Before becoming a middleweight title challenger, Cannonier was a heavyweight weighing more than 250 pounds while working in Alaska maintaining air traffic equipment.
 He arrived in the UFC with a 7-0 professional record, but his promotional debut against Shawn Jordan at UFC 182 in January 2015 ended in a first-round knockout defeat.
 He eventually found success against Cyril Asker before moving to light heavyweight in 2016. A victory over Ion Cuțelaba demonstrated his potential at 205 pounds, but defeats to Jan Błachowicz and Dominick Reyes suggested he had yet to find his ideal division.
 That changed in November 2018. Cannonier made an immediate impression at middleweight, stopping David Branch at UFC 230 before recording knockout victories over Anderson Silva and Jack Hermansson. His ability to carry his power down two weight classes transformed him into a legitimate contender.
 By July 2022, he was challenging Israel Adesanya for the middleweight championship at UFC 276. He lost a unanimous decision but had completed a remarkable journey from heavyweight to title challenger.
 Cannonier’s transformation was not exclusively physical. His striking evolved from explosive, power-oriented attacks into a more patient, high-volume approach capable of sustaining pressure over five rounds.
 His June 2023 victory over Marvin Vettori remains the clearest demonstration of that evolution. Cannonier landed 241 significant strikes, setting the UFC middleweight single-fight record.
 However, the results have become less convincing. After defeating Vettori, Cannonier lost to Nassourdine Imavov and Caio Borralho in 2024. He briefly recovered with a fourth-round TKO of Gregory Rodrigues in February 2025, but subsequent unanimous decision defeats to Michael Page and Christian Leroy Duncan extended his decline.
 He now enters Qatar with a 1-4 record across his last five appearances and a two-fight losing streak.
 Beyond UFC Qatar: Will Cannonier’s UFC Contract Be Renewed?
 Cannonier faces another difficult assignment against 33-year-old Ikram Aliskerov, who has won three consecutive fights.
 The betting markets favor Aliskerov, with Cannonier entering as the underdog. It is an understandable assessment given their recent trajectories, although Cannonier’s experience and knockout power make him a dangerous opponent.
 A victory would interrupt his losing streak and demonstrate that he can still compete against younger contenders. However, it may not be enough to convince the UFC that another contract is worthwhile.
 The contractual situation makes the fight particularly interesting. In July 2025, Cannonier stated that he had four fights remaining on his UFC deal ahead of his meeting with Page. The exact number remaining has not been publicly confirmed. If that original figure remained unchanged, Aliskerov would be his third fight since the announcement, leaving one bout on his deal.
 A defeat in Doha would make the situation considerably worse. A third consecutive loss, and fifth in six fights, would give the promotion little sporting reason to extend his contract.
 We would not be surprised if the UFC eventually decides against renewing his deal, particularly if he cannot turn things around against Aliskerov.
 Cannonier has already accomplished something extraordinary by reinventing himself across three weight classes and reaching championship level. But at 42, his next fight could determine whether the UFC sees him as a veteran still worth investing in or a former contender whose best years are behind him.
